paras: The lynching of Elijah Church took place on the night of October 6, 1881, when a body of men took Church, a white prisoner, from the jail at Newton, Catawba County, North Carolina, and hanged him to a tree outside the town. Church was awaiting trial on a charge of murdering a Miss Thompson in Alexander County that August. A wire dispatch carried the news to papers across the country, and North Carolina reports tied the lynching to the confession of a second accused man, E. H. Dockery.

Miss Thompson was killed in Alexander County in August 1881, and Church was charged with her murder. According to the Yorkville Enquirer's North Carolina column, he had first been held at Taylorsville and was moved to the Newton jail for safety. A second man implicated in the same killing, named Dockery in the Charlotte paper but printed as Rockery, Backney, Bereker or Pockery elsewhere, was held in the jail at Statesville.

At about ten o'clock on Thursday night, October 6, a body of 28 men, "not one of whom was disguised," rode into Newton. They demanded the keys of the jail from the jailor and took Church out. The men carried him about a mile and a half from the town and hanged him to a tree until he was dead. The wire filed from Lincolnton the next day reported only that he "was taken out and hanged by a mob last night" and that Dockery was feared to be next.

By October 21, Sheriff Mays of Alexander County had judged it unsafe to keep Dockery in the Alexander jail or any adjoining one and brought him to the Charlotte jail. The Charlotte Home and Democrat wrote that Church had been lynched "through Dockery's confession" and that Dockery's testimony was expected to implicate two others, one of whom, Adams, was under bond to appear at court. The paper concluded that "it was the friends of these that lynched Church," an inference it did not support with names or evidence. No report of an inquest or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

Most papers outside North Carolina printed the same short dispatch, credited to a special to the Wilmington Star from Lincolnton and dated October 7. Headline writers gave it heads ranging from "Mob Law in North Carolina" in the Savannah Morning News and "Lynched by a Mob" in the Chicago Tribune to the jocular "Necktie Social in North Carolina" in the Wheeling Intelligencer and "Work of a Tar-Heel Mob" in the Memphis Appeal. As the item moved into weekly news-in-brief columns, the qualifier "charged with" dropped away, and papers in Iowa, Missouri and Alabama called Church "the murderer of Miss Thompson" or a man "who murdered Miss Thompson."

Copying also introduced errors: the second accused's name took several forms, one brief placed the jail at Wilmington, the wire's dateline, and another gave the date as the 7th. A widely reprinted brief said "Citizens of Alexander County" had taken Church from prison, while the Iowa Plain Dealer credited "the people of Newton." Carolina papers, including the Newberry Herald, the Charlotte Home and Democrat and the Winston Western Sentinel, identified Church as "a white man," and only the Yorkville Enquirer described the riders, the jailor and the hanging place. None of these papers condemned the lynching in the items found.

Most reports, including the October 7 wire and the Carolina papers, place the lynching on the night of Thursday, October 6, while the Mower County Transcript dated it "the 7th inst.," apparently from the wire's date. Accounts of who acted also differ: the Yorkville Enquirer described 28 men who rode into Newton, other briefs named citizens of Alexander County or the people of Newton, and the Charlotte editor blamed friends of other suspects.

bases: A body of men took Church from the Newton jail and hanged him to a tree outside town (A18, A2, A22).

Twenty-eight men took Church, who was held on a murder charge, from jail and hanged him without any legal process (A18); the wire and the Charlotte paper agree he was hanged by a mob while charged with the murder of Miss Thompson (A2, A22).

The Wilmington/Lincolnton wire (A2, A1), the independent Yorkville 'North Carolina News' account (A18) and the Charlotte local items (A22, A28) agree that Church was taken from the Newton jail and hanged.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Oct 7 wire under heads like 'Mob Law in North Carolina', 'LYNCHED BY A MOB' or the jocular 'Necktie Social in North Carolina' and 'Work of a Tar-Heel Mob'.
Later briefs dropped the qualifier 'charged with' and called Church 'the murderer of Miss Thompson' or one 'who murdered Miss Thompson'.
The Charlotte paper reported the case without comment on the mob beyond attributing it to friends of other suspects.

conflicts.note: The Oct 6 date rests on the wire filed Oct 7 and on several independent 'Thursday night' reports; the 7th is likely the wire date.

versions.value: Friends of other implicated men (editor's inference)

conflicts.note: Only the Yorkville account gives a number; the men 'rode into Newton', which fits the Alexander county version better than the 'people of Newton'.
Wilmington was the wire dateline; the South Kentuckian brief appears to have mistaken it for the place.
The Charlotte paper, which reported his transfer to its own city's jail, gives Dockery.
